title: Five First Week Reflections
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: In this personal end-of-first-week dispatch, Dave Stuart Jr. shares five reflections from his eighteenth year of teaching, mixing candid fatigue with renewed encouragement. He walks through practical anchors for the opening days: learning 134 students' names one class period at a time, leaning into brief mini-sermons to explain why the work matters, using an index-card values activity to surface what students care about, and repeatedly communicating his classroom's Everest Statement. Throughout, he frames these small, repeatable moves as mutually reinforcing tools that build Credibility, Efficacy, and Belonging simultaneously. The piece closes with a note of gratitude to fellow teachers and a reaffirmation that, despite exhaustion, this will be a good year to teach.
points: Stuart tackles the challenge of learning 134 student names by focusing on "one class at a time" rather than trying to master the whole roster at once, using index cards and attentive reading of student writing to build recognition.
His first-day index-card activity doubles as a research-derived Values Affirmation exercise, giving him insight into students while quietly cultivating the Belonging belief.
Repeating the Everest Statement across the first week in varied formats functions as a triple signal, boosting Credibility, Efficacy, and the teacher's own motivation at once.
He credits a nearby school's laser focus on mini-sermons for pushing him to bring extra creativity and authenticity to his own brief, 30-to-60-second value-arguments.
quotes: But here's one thing I know: 134 is a lot of human beings to get to know in a week! Especially for an introverted guy like me.

When you read things they've written, picture their face as best you can. Find those connection points — the quicker you can attach meaning to their name and face, the quicker you'll gain a sense of knowing them as humans and not just as 134 people to get to know.
I needed to bring my A-game with mini-sermons because I knew they were. And I knew a bunch of other folks all around the country were doing it.
This serves the obvious benefit of giving me insight into the hearts of my students, though a real but invisible side benefit is that this cultivates the Belonging belief, too.

Everest Statements, like all the tools I recommend, are only as useful as we make them. And each time we practice communicating Everest, our skill improves, as does the likelihood that the Everest will sink in.
It's because of you that I've written my books, that I've travelled to a dozen or so schools this past summer, and continue to push forward my practice in the simple yet deep areas I write about.
